title: p0232
universal_lens: The kinematic release manifold of a rigid body throw is constrained by the angular velocity vector and the spatial arc. Minimizing lateral deviation requires projecting the release tangent onto the target axis, reducing the effective error subspace to vertical perturbations.
gsi_mapping: Bayesian inference models the release point as a latent variable with a posterior distribution over the impact coordinates. Conformal prediction intervals are tighter for straight-arm throws because the covariance matrix of the error distribution is heavily anisotropic, suppressing lateral variance.
gse_mapping: State-transition logic dictates that in-field throws must minimize flight time and maximize receiver state stability. The optimal control policy selects a linear trajectory to reduce the catcher's required reaction bandwidth when transitioning to a tag action.

reasoning_traces.think:
The foundational duality presented in the text maps directly to the geometry of error manifolds in high-dimensional kinematic spaces. Round-arm throwing operates on a two-dimensional circular arc, meaning the release event is highly sensitive to temporal perturbations. A slight delay in letting go translates the ball's velocity vector away from the intended target, creating large lateral deviations. This is mathematically equivalent to a steep gradient on the loss landscape. Conversely, straight-arm throwing collapses the primary degree of freedom into a linear extension. Here, the velocity vector remains largely aligned with the target axis even if the release timing fluctuates. The resulting error is predominantly vertical. Because the receiving apparatus (the baseman) can easily compensate for vertical variations—catching the ball slightly higher or lower—the effective cost function is significantly flatter. Furthermore, the rejection of side-arm styles highlights the importance of minimizing spin-induced Magnus forces, which introduce non-linear curvature and unpredictable bounce dynamics upon ground interaction. In-field constraints demand linear trajectories to minimize flight time and simplify the downstream state estimation for the catcher. When a runner slides low, the catcher's operational envelope is restricted to the ground plane. Therefore, keeping the throw 'down' ensures the ball arrives within the optimal interception volume, maximizing the probability of a successful tag. The primitives collectively formalize these biomechanical heuristics into rigorous operators governing trajectory optimization, error projection, and state-transition efficiency.
